alternates: Heat Pump vs Gas Furnace: Who Gets the Lower Bill?

stories.question: Is a heat pump actually cheaper to run than a gas furnace?
stories.whyWatch: Half the videos promise lower bills and the other half show bills going up, and both can be telling the truth. The national models, state prices and one large measured study show exactly which homes save and which pay more.
stories.tension: Advocates say a heat pump is three times as efficient, so it must be cheaper. Skeptics point out that electricity costs three to four times as much as gas per unit of energy. Both numbers are real, and they nearly cancel.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Measured or modelled bill changes for gas-heated homes after switching, broken down by equipment efficiency, location and tariff, plus state prices to show the break-even.

stories.premise: Running cost against gas comes down to one comparison: the heat pump's seasonal efficiency against the electricity-to-gas price ratio times the furnace's efficiency. At 2024 EIA prices a seasonal efficiency of 2.5 beats a 95% furnace in only 11 states, and 30 states need 3 or more. NREL's national model of 550,000 homes finds bills rise in 39% of homes with minimum-efficiency units and 5% with high-efficiency cold-climate units, so most homes save, but among gas-heated homes with AC the share that saves runs from 38% to 99% depending on the equipment, and is lower for gas homes without AC. These are models at 2021-22 prices. Edwards' county model finds 53% clearly save, 19% pay more and 28% show no clear change. The one large measured study is British: replacing gas boilers raised running costs about 190 pounds a year on a flat tariff, while a heat-pump time-of-use tariff saved about 318 pounds; its authors are linked to the supplier, and UK prices are not US prices. Promises of halving the bill fail for gas homes; RMI's US models find time-of-use rates help only with steep tariffs and smart control.

arc.hook: Two neighbours install the same heat pump. One's winter bill drops; the other's goes up. Neither is lying.
arc.conflict: Efficiency says a heat pump wins by three to one; prices say electricity costs three to four times as much as gas. Which number wins depends on where you live and what you buy.
arc.evidence: The break-even equation with real state prices, then the national models' share of homes that save by equipment tier, then the UK measured study and the tariff effect.
arc.resolution: Most gas homes save with efficient equipment where electricity is not too expensive; a cheap unit in a high-price state costs more to run. Halving the bill is not a realistic promise against gas.
arc.takeaway: Before switching, divide your electricity price by your gas price and compare it with the seasonal efficiency of the unit you are quoted.

coherence.explanation: One question, is a heat pump cheaper to run than a gas furnace, answered by what decides it (price ratio, efficiency), how often it comes out ahead, and the tariff lever. The oil, propane and resistance comparisons are a different question with their own story, and the gas connection fee is a footnote.

central.text: Time-of-use or heat-pump electricity tariffs make heat pumps cheaper to run

supporting.by: Bernard 2024 (NBER), UK heat pumps and a time-of-use tariff
supporting.note: Staggered-adoption study of 6,631 UK households: switching to Octopus's Cosy heat pump time-of-use tariff saved about £318/yr (about 18% of the electricity bill), £78 from the tariff structure alone and £240 from shifting load; savings are vs the same supplier's flat tariff, and the authors are linked to Octopus.
supporting.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

supporting.by: Mass Save 2026, air-source heat pump rebates
supporting.note: Mass Save: eligible customers can get a Seasonal Heat Pump Rate with lower electric rates November through April 'to help make heat pump operation more affordable'; time-of-use rates are only described as future options.
supporting.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

qualifying.by: RMI 2018, the economics of electrifying buildings
qualifying.note: In RMI's models a tariff alone does not cut costs: a standard heat pump on Houston's Free Nights rate costs more than on a flat rate, and only flexible control on steep tariffs (3:1 TOU, Free Nights) saved about $1,000-2,000 over 15 years, while mild default TOU gave too little.
qualifying.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

NREL's national model finds at most 55% of homes with positive unsubsidized lifetime value from a single heat pump tier, 59% if every home picked its best option, over 16 years; Deetjen finds 21% of single-family houses benefit at current costs. Both are models with their own price and discount assumptions, and both price the heat pump against replacing the old equipment like for like at the end of its life, so these shares are already the buy-at-replacement case, not the cost of tearing out working equipment. Payback varies with climate, fuel prices and what the heat pump replaces: homes heated with propane or electric resistance, and many with oil, are the clearest winners, though Deetjen finds oil homes often lose over the life once capital is counted. Envelope upgrades cut the share of homes whose bills rise but add enough upfront cost to help mainly in cold climates. Field data from Minnesota put payback at about a year when the old system needed replacing anyway and decades when it did not.

stories.premise: Field studies in occupied homes reject the claim that heat pumps do not work in cold climates: metered New England mini-splits kept an average COP of about 1.5 at -10 to 0F, prototype cold-climate units in the DOE challenge held a median COP of 1.9 at 0-5F, and Minnesota homes cut heating costs 30-56% against propane and electric resistance. Each study monitored a small number of homes, and none used gas as the baseline. Efficiency and capacity do fall, defrost cuts output, and backup resistance heat is the real cost risk: in NREL's 12 homes it used more than 40% as much energy as the heat pump at five sites, mostly undersized or faulty ones, and in the DOE challenge it ran a quarter of the time below 0F. Against gas, a dual-fuel setup can be cheapest, but at Massachusetts prices the older units tested never beat gas, so the switchover point depends on the unit and local prices.

arc.hook: It's -10F outside. Is the heat pump still heating, or is it just an expensive space heater now?
arc.conflict: The myth says heat pumps quit in the cold; the marketing says they work at -15F with no compromise. Neither describes what the meters show.
arc.evidence: COP by temperature bin from metered homes, capacity at the coldest readings, defrost and backup runtime, and the sites where backup heat took over.
arc.resolution: Modern units keep heating well below 0F at lower efficiency; the bill risk comes from backup heat, which proper sizing and controls keep small.
arc.takeaway: In a cold climate, buy a cold-climate unit sized for heating, and watch how often the backup runs.

stories.premise: From 2023 through 2025 the 25C federal credit covered 30% of a qualifying heat pump up to $2,000; the IRS confirms it does not apply to property placed in service after December 31, 2025, so it cannot be claimed for 2026 installs, and it was nonrefundable. The IRA's income-limited rebates depend on state programs that rolled out slowly, and they were never available to most homeowners. DOE Program Notice 26-2, effective May 29, 2026, removed fuel-switching from the electric appliance rebate: it now pays only to replace electric equipment, although reservations already made are honored and states have months to comply. State and utility rebates remain and can be substantial, as in Massachusetts' per-ton rebates, but in LBNL's project data the median rebate covered about a fifth of gross cost, so they reduce the price rather than erase it. Rebates making a heat pump cheaper upfront than furnace plus AC is possible in generous programs but is not the typical case.

arc.hook: That video promising a $2,000 tax credit? The credit is gone.
arc.conflict: The incentive landscape changed twice in a year, and most of what homeowners have heard is out of date.
arc.evidence: The IRS end date, the DOE notice text, the state rollout tracker, and real rebate shares from project data.
arc.resolution: The federal credit ended after 2025 and the federal rebate no longer pays for gas-to-heat-pump swaps; state and utility programs are what remains.
arc.takeaway: Check your state energy office and utility before getting quotes, and ignore any federal credit promised for a 2026 install.

stories.question: Should you replace a gas furnace that still works, or wait until it or the AC dies?
stories.whyWatch: The same heat pump can pay back in about a year or take decades, and the difference is not the equipment, it is the timing. This is the decision most homeowners actually face.

stories.premise: Payback should count only what a heat pump costs beyond the system you would buy anyway. Replacing a working gas furnace carries the whole cost and rarely pays back on energy alone; lifetime models agree. When the air conditioner needs replacing, the extra cost is the gap between a heat pump and an AC, about $1,500 or 30% at national medians in Edwards' data; NREL finds the wholesale gap is $200 to $500 but whole-home heating sizing raises it. In Minnesota field data, payback was about one year when both furnace and AC needed replacing and 15 to 29 years when nothing did, from a small sample against propane and resistance heat. Adding a heat pump beside a working furnace cuts fuel use, but CEE found integrating with older furnaces was complicated and most needed new ones, and no study here quantifies the fuel saving against gas. If you keep the furnace, a new AC costs less upfront than a heat pump, at least for efficient equipment.

arc.hook: Your furnace is 12 years old and works fine. A contractor says switch now. Should you?
arc.conflict: Switch-now advocates count the whole bill savings; wait-and-see skeptics count the whole installed price. The right comparison is neither.
arc.evidence: Payback with and without a needed replacement in the field data, the heat pump versus AC cost gap, and what happens when a heat pump is added beside a working furnace.
arc.resolution: Wait for a replacement, ideally the AC: then a heat pump costs little extra and pays back quickly. Tearing out a working furnace rarely pays on energy savings alone.
arc.takeaway: Plan the switch now, but buy it when the AC or furnace needs replacing.
